sections.title: Temperature Control and Vessel Geometry
body: Precise temperature control on a jacketed reactor comes down to how well the vessel and jacket actually fit together, not just how powerful the circulator running through them is.

Reactor-Ready Flex's vessel geometry and jacket design are optimised specifically to deliver accurate, consistent control across the full -70°C to +230°C range, rather than relying on raw circulator output to compensate for a loose thermal fit. That range is wider than Radleys' own Mya 4 reaction station line, which makes Flex the choice when a reaction genuinely needs to go colder or hotter than a multi-zone screening station reaches.

longForm.heroLead: React and filter in the same vessel. The batch never moves between them. Isolating a solid from a slurry usually means moving the batch somewhere else to filter it. That transfer is where product gets lost, and where temperature control gets harder to hold. This vessel is jacketed all the way down to the filter plate, so temperature control doesn't stop when filtration starts. The zero-dead-space bottom outlet valve and swivel filter support keep product loss and hassle to a minimum, and the whole filter assembly comes apart and goes back together tool-free, in minutes. Already running a Reactor-Ready framework? Upgrade it to accept filter vessels directly, or start with a dedicated Filter Reactor built for this from the ground up. Either way, AVA software logs temperature, stirring, and pH automatically through the whole process.

body: The core idea is no transfer step. Reaction and filtration happen in the same vessel, which is where the yield and temperature-control benefit both come from.
The jacket doesn't stop at the reaction zone. It extends all the way down to the filter plate, holding temperature control through filtration itself.
Product loss is engineered out, not just minimized. A zero-dead-space bottom outlet valve and a filter plate with removable clamp both target this directly.
Membrane choice comes as an evaluation kit, not a guess. One each of six styles, pre-cut, with the option to cut your own material to size.
Filter plate material is a real tradeoff. PTFE covers -30 to +120°C; PEEK extends that to -30 to +180°C at similar chemical compatibility.
Assembly is tool-free and fast. A swivel filter support plate aligns everything, even holding the plate and cake in place when the clamp is unlocked.
You don't have to start from zero. Existing Reactor-Ready frameworks can be upgraded to accept filter vessels directly.

sections.title: Jacketed Filter Vessel Engineering
body: Every part of this vessel's design targets one of two problems: losing temperature control during filtration, or losing product to the equipment itself.

The jacket runs the full height down to the filter plate, not just around the reaction zone, which is what keeps temperature control consistent through both steps. The bottom outlet valve is built with zero dead space specifically to stop material collecting below the filter media, and it's removable for cleaning with a 15 mm bore for easy run-off. The seal between vessel and lid, an FEP-encapsulated O-ring with a PTFE collar on the DN100 flange, is what keeps the whole system leak-tight under those conditions.

sections.title: Single vs Double Circulator Configuration
body: The manifold kit you choose decides whether your two vessels share a temperature or run apart, and that choice is worth making deliberately.

The single circulator kit (RR121305) routes one thermoregulator to both vessels, holding them at the same temperature, and includes a blanking plug for running just one vessel when the second isn't needed. The double circulator kit (RR121310) routes two independent thermoregulators to the vessels, letting each run its own temperature entirely. The hose lengths differ between the two kits, 70 cm on the single and 60 cm on the double, reflecting the different manifold layouts.

faqs.question: What are Custom Jacketed Reaction Systems used for?

faqs.question: When should I choose custom instead of a standard Reactor-Ready system?
faqs.answer: Choose custom when your process needs a non-standard vessel geometry, special features like optical windows or split jackets, a system type like a fermenter or bioreactor, or a temperature and connection combination the standard range doesn't cover.

faqs.question: How do I scope a custom jacketed reaction system?

faqs.question: How do I decide between Reactor-Ready and traditional connections?
faqs.answer: Choose Reactor-Ready connections if you need to reach up to 230°C, or traditional connections if 200°C covers your process and a conventional setup is preferred.

faqs.question: What is the maximum volume for a custom system?

faqs.question: Can I get an air-powered stirrer for a hazardous atmosphere?
faqs.answer: Yes. Air-powered stirring is a confirmed option specifically for applications where an electrical motor poses an ignition risk.

faqs.question: Does Radleys build fermenters and bioreactors, not just standard reactors?

faqs.question: Is training included with a custom system?

longForm.heroLead: If a standard reactor doesn't fit, we build one that does. 50+ years of glassblowing behind it. Every process eventually runs into a requirement a catalog reactor wasn't designed for: an unusual geometry, a hazardous atmosphere, a vessel that needs to see light through it. This is where Radleys' own design engineers and scientific glassblowers take over, with over 50 years of experience building for industrial and academic research facilities worldwide. The scope runs from a small benchtop reactor to a complex multi-vessel parallel rig, 100 mL to 30 litres, built to your specification and budget. Cylindrical or spherical vessels, conical or dish or hemispherical bottoms, optical windows, split jackets, fixed or removable filters. Fermenters, bioreactors, photoreactors, distillation assemblies. Electrical or air-powered stirring, for atmospheres where an electrical motor isn't an option. Connection type genuinely changes what's achievable: Reactor-Ready connections reach 230°C; traditional connections cap at 200°C.

sections.title: Vessel and System Customization Options
body: Two levels of customization apply here: the vessel itself, and the system it sits within.

At the vessel level, shape (cylindrical or spherical), bottom geometry (conical, dish, or hemispherical), and special features (optical windows, split jackets, fixed or removable filters) are all confirmed options, not exceptions requiring special approval. At the system level, the scope extends well past a single reactor: multi-reactor rigs for parallel synthesis, fermenters and bioreactors for biological work, photoreactors for light-driven chemistry, and supporting equipment like condensers, distillation assemblies, and scrubbers.
